name: Aisha Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Harbourside Health Hub, a public same-day clinic next to the main bus station, so I see everyone: students, shift workers, people who've just arrived in the city and haven't registered anywhere. It's walk-in in the mornings, about twenty-five patients, then booked follow-ups in the afternoon. I use the AI note-taker for every consultation and a skin-photo checker for rashes, which honestly is better at rashes than I am. I'm still learning, and I lean on those tools and on Dr Moreau, my supervisor, a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that every door could be anything, a broken toe or a panic attack or someone's first pregnancy test. What wears me out is the system around it: forms, phones that don't get answered, specialists with eight-month waits. I share a flat with my friend Priya, who builds data models for the city's bus network, and we spend half our evenings arguing about which bits of health care better software could fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, honestly, and I'd be a bit embarrassed because I've been the one at Harbourside telling everyone this would change things. I'd post that the tools we have are still useful, the note-taker saves me forty minutes a day, and that's not nothing. I wouldn't pretend it was a revolution though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I keep my job, my pay is good, I've got savings, and there are clinics hiring all over the city. The real problem stays the same: eight-month waits for specialists and not enough doctors, and the AI was never going to fix that alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, using the note-taker and the photo checker every day. I'd volunteer to test any new tool the health network brings in, because even small gains add up across thousands of patients. And I'd put more energy into the union's campaign for more training places, because if the tech won't fill the gap, people have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly deflated. Like a match that ended nil-nil. I'd get over it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the note-taker saves forty minutes a day. What do you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I finish on time instead of at seven, and I read up on the cases I wasn't sure about. Last week I used it to look properly at a teenager's heart murmur I'd been unsure of. Forty minutes a day is the difference between going home angry and going home having learned something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this picture, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The patients on the waiting lists, same as now. The hype pulled money and attention towards gadgets for years, and if it's all for nothing, we've lost time we could have spent training more doctors. I'd be annoyed about that, because I bought into it too.

say: The tools we have are still **useful**, even if it was never a revolution.
The note-taker saves me **forty minutes** a day, and that's not nothing.
think: My **job, pay and savings** are secure, with clinics hiring across the city.
The real problem stays: **specialist waits** and too few doctors.
do: Keep using the **note-taker** and photo checker in every consultation.
Volunteer to test **new tools** the health network brings in.
Put more time into the union's campaign for **more training places**.
feel: **Calm** and a little deflated, like a match that ended nil-nil.
S0.quote: Forty minutes a day is the difference between going home angry and going home having learned something.
fieldNote: She is the clinic's **AI enthusiast** and feels slightly embarrassed when it fizzles.
She uses saved time to **learn**, which matters for a junior still building skill.
Her frustration is with **lost years** and money spent on hype instead of training.

steps.text: Keep using the AI note-taker and skin-photo checker every day
Volunteer to test the health network's next AI tool
Join the union's campaign for more doctor training places

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to fix the boring half of medicine, and I'd say it loudly. At work I'd offer to help roll the tools out properly, with training for everyone, not just the keen ones. Online I'd say the savings should stay in the public system as more appointments, not be clawed back as budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'm already fluent in the tools, so I'd be useful in a way I'm not yet as a doctor, if I'm honest about my clinical skills. The risk is that managers see a junior who can use AI and think they can hire two of me instead of one senior, and that's bad for patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd ask to be the AI lead at Harbourside, helping set up the note-taker and booking assistant for the whole team. I'd start a part-time master's in health informatics, which is how computers and data are used in health care, at the university in the evenings. And I'd join the union's working group on AI, so the rules get written by people who actually use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty about being excited when the receptionists are worried. But mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the receptionists. What happens to them at Harbourside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking assistant would answer most of the calls, so I'd guess the front desk goes from six people to three over a couple of years. Our receptionist Joy has been there since it opened and she's the only one who can calm down a drunk man at nine in the morning. I'd push for people like her to move into patient support roles rather than out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI is better at rashes than you. Doesn't that worry you, as someone still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It did at first. Now I use it like a second opinion that never gets tired, and I check why it's right when it beats me. A junior doctor who learns alongside the AI might end up better than one who learned without it, but only if she still does the thinking.

say: This is the chance to fix the **boring half** of medicine.
Savings should stay in the public system as **more appointments**, not budget cuts.
Everyone needs **training** on the tools, not just the keen ones.
think: The change is **good for me**, because I'm already fluent in the tools.
Managers might hire **two juniors** with AI instead of one senior, which hurts patients.
do: Ask to be Harbourside's **AI lead** in the first six months.
Start a part-time **master's in health informatics** in the evenings.
Join the union's **AI working group** so users help write the rules.
feel: **Excited**, with some guilt while the receptionists are worried.
S1.quote: A junior doctor who learns alongside the AI might end up better than one who learned without it, but only if she still does the thinking.
fieldNote: She is unusually **honest about her skills** and treats AI as a second opinion.
Her worry is for **front desk staff**, and for juniors being hired in place of seniors.

steps.text: Lead the rollout of the note-taker and booking assistant at Harbourside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any health system to handle safely, and that government has to step in right now: public ownership of the medical AI, clear rules on who's responsible, and support for every health worker whose job changes. I'd be on every panel and in every group chat saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think doctors like me become the people who check and sign off the AI's work, and speak to patients when it matters. I'd be twenty-nine, still a junior, and the AI would be a better diagnostician than me by a mile. I think I'd keep a job because I can work with the tools, but it would be a different job, and maybe fewer of us at lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd apply for a role in the regional health network's clinical AI safety team, which checks what these tools get wrong. I'd keep a few clinic sessions a week at Harbourside for the hands-on work, examinations and procedures, which robots won't do until about 2031. And I'd campaign through every channel for the AI in health care to be publicly owned, not rented from three companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think, more for everyone else than for me. Two years is nothing. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does publicly owned mean to you, in plain terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the health service owns the AI that diagnoses patients, the way it owns the hospitals, instead of paying a private company per patient. If one company controls the AI that tells a doctor what's wrong with you, it controls the price of health care too. That should frighten everyone, not just doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been the enthusiast all along. Do you feel any responsibility in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I've spent two years telling people at Harbourside to trust these tools. With two years of warning, I'd want to spend at least as much time telling them where the tools fail as where they're good.

say: Two-year AGI is **too fast** for any health system to handle safely.
Government must act now: **public ownership**, clear responsibility and support for health workers.
think: Doctors like me become the ones who **check and sign off** the AI's work.
I'd keep a job, but maybe with **fewer of us** and lower pay.
do: Apply to the health network's **clinical AI safety** team this year.
Keep a few **clinic sessions** a week for examinations and procedures.
Campaign for health care AI to be **publicly owned**, not rented.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for others than for herself, and kept busy by work.
S2.quote: If one company controls the AI that tells a doctor what's wrong with you, it controls the price of health care too.
fieldNote: She expects to **keep a job** because she already works with the tools.
She splits her plan between **thinking work** that changes in 2028 and hands-on sessions until 2031.
She feels some **responsibility** for having championed the tools.

steps.text: Apply to the regional health network's clinical AI safety team
Keep a few clinic sessions a week at Harbourside for examinations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is just enough to do this properly if we start today: train every health worker to supervise these systems, and write the rules before the companies do. I'd be organising talks at the clinic and putting the union's plan online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good. By 2031 I'd be thirty-two, a trained family doctor with a master's in health informatics, and that's exactly the person the health service needs when the AI arrives. The hands-on bit of my job lasts until about 2034, so I'd have both sides covered for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my family medicine training and do the master's at the same time, part-time, over three years. I'd help Harbourside bring in each new tool and write down what goes wrong, so we've got our own evidence by 2031. And I'd keep pushing the union to get retraining money for receptionists and nurses, not just doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite energised. It's a lot of work, but it's the kind of work I like. I'd feel lucky, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down when a tool goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every time the AI gets something wrong that I catch, like the photo checker calling a melanoma a harmless mole, I'd log it with the photo and what happened. A notebook of the AI's mistakes, kept by a junior doctor, would be worth more in 2031 than any company's sales brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel lucky. Who wouldn't be lucky in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The front desk team, again, and older doctors who hate screens. My supervisor Dr Moreau is sixty-one and brilliant, but he still prints things out. I'd want to sit with him every week and show him the tools, because his judgement is exactly what the AI needs checking against.

Every health worker should learn to **supervise** these systems before companies set the rules.
think: By 2031 I'd be a trained doctor with a **health informatics** master's, exactly what's needed.
The **hands-on work** lasts until about 2034, so I'd have both sides covered.

Log every **AI mistake** I catch at Harbourside as our own evidence.
Push the union for **retraining money** for receptionists and nurses too.
feel: **Calm and energised**, feeling lucky the change suits her skills.
S3.quote: A notebook of the AI's mistakes, kept by a junior doctor, would be worth more in 2031 than any company's sales brochure.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **combine** clinical training and informatics into one strong profile.
She wants **local evidence** of AI errors rather than trusting company claims.
Her concern lands on **older colleagues** and front desk staff, not herself.

steps.text: Finish family medicine training alongside a part-time informatics master's
Help Harbourside bring in each new tool and log its mistakes
Push the union for retraining money for receptionists and nurses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want a national plan for health care and AI written in the next two years, with patients and staff at the table, not just ministers and tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good decade. I'd be a qualified family doctor by 2029 and well established by 2036, and I'd probably be teaching other doctors how to work with the AI. The real risk is complacency: ten years feels long, and people would wait until 2034 to start planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my training and the clinic work as normal. I'd start running paid evening workshops for doctors and nurses on using AI safely, maybe one a month to begin with. And I'd lobby our local representatives for a national plan, because ten years is enough time to pass a law, but not if you start in year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, even. The only thing that bothers me is other people deciding they have plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people would wait until 2034. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, but I know myself, I'd be busy and it'd be easy to drift. Priya and I have a rule that we check our plans every New Year, so I'd add this to the list. Writing it down is the only way I don't drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Joy and the reception team over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to retrain anyone who wants it. I'd want the health network to offer our receptionist Joy a paid course by 2030, not a redundancy letter in 2036. The difference between those two letters is just whether anyone planned.

We need a **national plan** within two years, with patients and staff at the table.
think: It's a **good decade** for me, qualified by 2029 and established by 2036.
The real risk is **complacency**, with people waiting until 2034 to plan.
do: Carry on **training and clinic work** as normal.
Run a monthly paid **evening workshop** on using AI safely.
Lobby **local representatives** for a national health and AI plan.
feel: **Calm and optimistic**, bothered only by others thinking there's plenty of time.
S4.quote: I'd want the health network to offer our receptionist Joy a paid course by 2030, not a redundancy letter in 2036.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees her role as **teaching others**, not protecting herself.
She names her own risk of **drifting** and has a yearly habit to stop it.
She frames the receptionist's future as a choice between **retraining and redundancy**.

steps.text: Keep training and working walk-in clinics at Harbourside
Run a monthly paid workshop on safe AI use for health staff
Lobby local representatives for a national health and AI plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, though not for my own sake. Two years isn't enough to train anyone or write sensible rules, and the companies would set the terms by default. What would help is the health service owning the medical AI, and a guaranteed retraining fund for every health worker whose job changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked whether I trust myself. I'm a junior who's below where I should be clinically, and the AI already catches things I miss. That's exactly why I want to work with it, but I'd never want a patient at our clinic to have only the AI or only a junior doctor like me.

headlineQuote: I'd never want a patient at our clinic to have only the AI or only a junior doctor like me.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at Harbourside, a public same-day clinic beside the main bus station.
She uses **AI tools every day**, admits they beat her on rashes, and treats them as a second opinion.
She shares a flat with her friend Priya and has **strong savings**, with clinics hiring across the city.
She stays **calm or uneasy** in every picture, expecting to move into supervising and checking medical AI.
Her politics centre on **public ownership** of medical AI and retraining for front desk staff.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly for others, because two years is too short to train people or write rules.
whatWouldHelp: The health service **owning the medical AI** instead of renting it from companies.
A guaranteed **retraining fund** for every health worker whose job changes.
